With spiritual consolation of the soul, I
have reviewed this little book, titled
*Holy Soul’s Delight*. It may be quite
properly and usefully brought to light
through public printing for the increase of
love and the praise of God.
Wrocław <note>original: "Breßlaw"</note>, the 1st of May,
in the year 1657 <note>original: "Anno 1657"</note>.

## The Soul in Love.

I give you here these **Spiritual Pastoral Songs** <note>original: *Geistliche Hirten-Lieder*. A popular 17th-century literary genre where spiritual devotion was expressed through metaphors of shepherds, flocks, and idyllic nature.</note> and the loving desires of the **Bride of Christ** <note>A traditional mystical concept representing the individual soul or the Church in a devoted relationship with Christ.</note> for her **Groom**; with which you may delight yourself according to your pleasure and, in the wilderness of this world, like a **chaste turtledove**, you can sigh inwardly and sweetly for **Jesus**, your Beloved. It would be a mockery for us if we allowed those who are in love with the world—who sing and speak so much of their base and blind love—to outdo us, and did not also sing something of the love of our sweet God. For although many beautiful

<summary>In this preface, the author presents his collection of spiritual pastoral songs to the reader, encouraging them to use the verses to express their intimate devotion to Christ. He justifies the work by arguing that spiritual love deserves at least as much poetic expression as the worldly love celebrated by secular poets.</summary>
<keywords>Soul in Love, Bride of Christ, spiritual longing, pastoral poetry, Baroque devotion, Jesus Christ, worldliness vs. spirituality</keywords>

## A Reminder to the Reader.

Beloved reader/ in this little book, there are several melodies here and there which were not invented by us; but rather were adopted by the author <term>Urheber: The "author" or creator of the work, referring to the person who compiled or wrote the text and music.</term> for certain reasons. And although their inventors are not known to us/ I have nevertheless found it good to let you know this/ so that you do not think/ we wished to adorn ourselves with borrowed feathers <note>The idiom "adorn oneself with borrowed feathers" (German: *mit fremden Federn zieren*) is a classical reference to Aesop's fables, meaning to take credit for another's work.</note>/ and pass them off as our own. Receive this kindly/ and fare thee well. If we perceive, however, that this work pleases you/ then in the future you shall receive most of our melodies with beautiful symphonies <term>Symphonien: In the 17th century, "symphony" usually referred to instrumental introductory pieces or interludes within a vocal work, rather than a full orchestral symphony.</term> and full-voiced instruments <term>Instrumenten: General term for musical instruments, likely referring here to strings or winds used in church settings.</term> for public church use <term>Kirchen-Brauch: Literally "church-custom," referring to the established liturgy or practice of the church.</term>.

<summary>The author concludes a spiritual dedication to Jesus and provides an honest disclaimer to the reader about the musical melodies, explaining that some are borrowed rather than original compositions. He promises more elaborate instrumental arrangements in future editions if the current work is successful.</summary>

<keywords>Jesus Christ, melodies, authorship, church music, symphonies, musical instruments, hymns</keywords>

# Index and Contents of the Shepherd Songs.

1. Psyche <term>Psyche: In Baroque literature, "Psyche" (the Greek word for "soul") is an allegory for the individual human soul in its relationship with the Divine.</term> sighs for her Jesus like a lonely turtledove for her mate.
2. She calls for her Beloved out of longing.
3. She yearns for Jesus alone.
4. She seeks the Beloved of her soul.
5. She complains to Him about His long absence.
6. She calls Him by many sweet names.
7. She calls Him again with great desire.
8. She holds Jesus as her jewel <note>The word "Kleinod" refers to a precious treasure or a piece of jewelry, symbolizing Christ's immense value to the soul.</note>.
9. She scorns the world and turns to her Jesus.
10. She promises to love Him until death.
11. She desires Him at the rising of the sun.
12. She asks the creatures <note>Referring to all created things in nature (animals, plants, elements) as witnesses to the Creator's beauty.</note> about her Bridegroom.
13. She longs for the spiritual birth of Jesus Christ/ and prays/ that such might occur in her heart.
14. She prepares herself for His birth.
15. She praises the Virginal Mother of her Bridegroom.
16. She bids the Infant Jesus <term>JEsulein: A diminutive form of endearment for the infant Jesus, common in German devotional poetry to express intimacy and tenderness.</term> welcome.
17. She sings of the greatness of His love.
18. She praises the loveliness of the Infant Jesus.
19. She caresses the Infant Jesus.
20. Psyche offers gifts to the Infant Jesus.
21. She greets the Infant Jesus with beautiful titles of honor.
22. She desires to kiss the Infant Jesus.
23. She rejoices over the birth of Jesus Christ.
24. She sings of the benefit of His birth.
25. She is full of joy in contemplation of the great treasures which His birth brings with it.
26. She wants to have the Infant Jesus as the true Morning Star <note>A traditional biblical title for Christ, signifying the dawn of salvation.</note> in the heaven of her heart.

And must by a little maiden <note>original: *Mägdelein*. Referring to the Virgin Mary; the diminutive form emphasizes the humble, human nature of the Nativity.</note>
Be held and carried,
Consoled by her lips.

->3.<-

There he was equal to God in power,
Could compel all spirits;
Nothing will be conceived in eternity
That could bring him unrest:
Now he has become a little lamb <note>original: *Lämblein*. A reference to the *Agnus Dei* (Lamb of God), signifying Christ's role as the sacrificial victim who takes away the sins of the world.</note>;
So that for me he shall be slain
By the enemy of my soul <note>original: *Seelen feind*. A common Baroque designation for the Devil or Satan.</note>,
Who intends to tear me to pieces.

->4.<-

O God, how great is the fervor <note>original: *Brunst*. In 17th-century devotional language, this term describes an intense, burning spiritual passion or divine love rather than its modern secular connotation.</note>,
With which Jesus loves me!
From eternity such favor
No one has ever shown so!
It was he alone:
Therefore, Jesus, my soul’s adornment <note>original: *Seelen Ziehr*. A poetic term for Christ as the one who beautifies or sanctifies the believer's inner life.</note>,
You alone can also help me,
Through you I must be healed.

**Vocabulary**
Son of God, manger, little maiden, eternity, little lamb, enemy of the soul, Jesus, fervor, soul’s adornment.

### 1.

Come out, all you virgins <note>A reference to the faithful soul or the "Daughter of Zion," common in bridal mysticism to represent the collective church or the individual believer.</note>
To gaze upon your King:
Behold him in his crown
Which he wears with great mockery <note>original: "Hohne." Refers to the scornful intent of the crown of thorns, meant to lampoon his title as "King of the Jews."</note>
For your sin and transgression.

### 2.

Behold how he is led forth,
How he is arrayed <note>original: "staffieret." While this usually means to be finely dressed, here it is used ironically to describe the mocking costume of the purple robe and crown of thorns.</note>!
Behold his misery and his suffering
On the day of his joys,
In his soul’s wedding-feast! <note>A central theme in 17th-century devotion: the cross is the "wedding bed" where Christ unites with the human soul.</note>

### 3.

Behold his face full of wounds,
Full of welts, full of sores!
Behold how his locks hang
Without adornment, without splendor,
Mingled with filth <note>original: "Koth." Refers to mud, dirt, or excrement, emphasizing the physical degradation of the scene.</note> and with blood!

### 4.

Behold how his neck is torn,
And is battered with scourges!
Behold the chains and the bonds
Which he wears as a pledge <note>original: "Unterpfande." A legal or financial term for a security or down-payment; here, Christ's physical bonds are the guarantee of humanity's spiritual freedom.</note>!
Consider his purple robe!

<term>Spiritual Shepherd-Songs</term>: The title of the collection, indicating hymns written in a pastoral style where the relationship between God and the soul is often compared to a shepherd and his flock or a bride and groom.
<term>Stem of the Cross</term>: A poetic reference to the wood of the crucifix.
<term>Look, Bride</term>: An invitation for the soul to engage in "Beholding," a form of meditation where one vividly imagines the scenes of the Passion.
<term>Bridegroom</term>: A title for Jesus used to express the intimate, loving bond between the Savior and the believer.
<term>Pain</term>: Refers to the "Schmertz" (sorrow/agony) of the Crucifixion.
<term>Wounds</term>: A central focus of Baroque devotion, where the wounds of Christ were seen as shelters for the soul.

->1.<-

I live now no longer; for Christ is my life, <note>original: "denn Christus ist mein Leben." A paraphrase of Galatians 2:20.</note>

->2.<-

My heart also does not burn for splendor and vain ornaments;
No wealth, money, or goods can
Blind my mind and spirit,
Because my Love is crucified.

->3.<-

That which is temporal <note>Referring to worldly things that exist only in time and eventually perish.</note> can bring me no joy;
The beauty of the flesh and its glory
Seem to me like a pale flower;
Because my Love is crucified.

->4.<-

The world need no longer trouble itself with me;
It will not draw my heart to its love:
I love and kiss even in death
The sweet Jesus, my God,
To whom my Love is crucified.

# Third Book.

### 1.

Where do you wish to go, since it is evening,
Beloved Pilgrim Jesus Christ?
Oh, do stay here and rest in me;
I will not let you go, you eternal Light;
I cry after you with a thousand sighs <note>original: "Ach." In Baroque devotional poetry, this exclamation represents the "sighs of the soul," a rhetorical device used to express intense spiritual longing.</note>;
Oh, stay here, my Life;
I want to give you lodging <note>original: "Herberg." This refers to the "inn" or "shelter" of the believer's heart, mirroring the hospitality offered to Christ at Emmaus.</note>.

### 2.

The sun has already set,
The night is here, which oppresses me;
Do come in, my Light of Joy,
Kindle my heart like a candle,
Illuminate it entirely with your radiance,
So that I may recognize you
And be set aflame through and through.

### 3.

If you stay with me, worthy guest,
Then I shall be freed of my burden;
You break bread for me in time of hunger <note>A reference to the "Breaking of the Bread" (Luke 24:30-31), the moment the disciples finally recognized the risen Christ.</note>,
You drive vanity far away,
You show me the right path,
You grant that my senses
May find the truth.

<term>Warheit (Truth)</term>: The spiritual clarity achieved when Christ "opens the eyes" of the believer.

### The Eighty-Third [Song].

# She Directs Her Soul toward True Rest.

<note>The following section contains musical notation intended for devotional singing, a common practice in 17th-century spiritual life where music was used to elevate the soul's meditation.</note>

<image-desc>Musical notation for two voices (likely Soprano and Bass) printed on five-line staves using diamond-shaped notes (mensural notation). The music includes C-clefs and F-clefs, time signatures, and barlines. The lyrics are interspersed between the staves.</image-desc>

My soul, do you wish to rest; and always delight yourself in God, <note>original: "gůttlich thun"; literally "to do divinely," meaning to enjoy spiritual well-being or to feast upon divine grace.</note>
do you desire from burdens <note>original: "Beschwerden"; the physical and spiritual weights of earthly life.</note> and cravings <note>original: "Begihrden"; the restless, worldly passions that disturb inner peace.</note>
to be set free; love Jesus and nothing else.

<term>Soul</term> (Seele) — the inner spiritual essence of a person which, in mystical tradition, is often personified as a bride seeking her groom, Christ.
<term>Rest</term> (Ruhe) — a central concept in Pietist and mystical thought, referring to *Gelassenheit* or the stillness of the heart when it stops seeking worldly things.

### 1.

You blissful **Good** that feeds all spirits /
And shows all creatures grace and favor;
When will you enter into me /
And fill [me] abundantly?
When will you be my life yourself /
And still all my desires?
<note>original: "Begehren stilln." To "still" desire is a recurring theme in 17th-century mysticism, suggesting that the restless soul only finds peace when it ceases its worldly seeking and rests in God.</note>

### 2.

You true **Paradise** / you eternal **Spring-**
**Garden**,
You broad flower-field of unheard-of kinds;
When will I from the desert earth
Be moved into your delight?
When will I become worthy of you /
And be eternally delighted by you?

### 3.

You joy-rich **Ray** when will you
enrapture me /
<note>original: "verzucken." This term describes a state of spiritual ecstasy or being "caught up" out of one's physical senses into a divine vision.</note>
And swallow me entirely into you / and your lightning?
When does the little spark, my soul,
Fall into the fire of your **Godhead**?
When shall it, together with its body-cave,
<note>original: "Leibes-Höle." A common mystical metaphor viewing the physical body as a dark cave or prison from which the soul's light seeks to merge with the divine sun.</note>
Be a single flame with you?

### 4.

You eternal **Sea of Delight** when will you
truly quench my thirst /
<note>original: "tränken." Literally "to water" or "to give drink to," implying a deep saturation of the soul.</note>
When will you sink me into yourself with body and soul?

<vocab>Good, Spirits, Creatures, Paradise, Spring-Garden, Soul, Godhead, Sea of Delight</vocab>

<meta>catchword: When</meta>

<summary>This page contains four stanzas of a mystical hymn where the soul addresses God through various metaphors—Paradise, a Ray of Light, and a Sea of Delight—longing for total immersion in the Divine. The text emphasizes the "Spark of the Soul" merging into the divine fire.</summary>
<keywords>mystical union, Seelenfünklein, spiritual ecstasy, divine longing, metaphors for God, 17th-century poetry</keywords>

<meta>This is the title page for the fourth part of a collection of spiritual hymns and poems, continuing the collaborative work of the poet Angelus Silesius and the composer Georg Joseph.</meta>

# JOHANN ANGELUS <note>original: "Johannis Angeli." This is the Latinized name of Johannes Scheffler (1624–1677), a famous German mystic and physician better known by his pen name, Angelus Silesius.</note>
### and
# GEORG JOSEPH <note>original: "Georgii Josephi." A composer and musician in Breslau who collaborated closely with Scheffler to set his poems to music.</note>
### Fourth Part
## Of the Spiritual
# Shepherd Songs/ <term>Hirten-Lieder: Pastoral songs. In the Baroque era, the "Shepherd" motif was often used to represent the soul's simple, rustic, and pure love for God.</term>
## belonging to the enamored Psyche. <note>In this context, "Psyche" represents the human soul in its mystical pursuit of divine love, modeled after the classical myth of Cupid and Psyche.</note>
### Consisting of all sorts of beautiful reflections and new melodies.

Only do not forget me / return soon to me /
You life of my spirit / and my soul’s adornment.

# Spiritual Shepherd Songs <note>original: 'Geistlicher Hirten-Lieder'. This collection by Johann Rist (1607–1667) was one of the most influential German hymnbooks of the 17th century, often blending pastoral themes with deep spiritual reflection.</note>

->1.<-

O Eternity! O Eternity!
My heart must weep within me /
When it considers the infinity of your time
And your torments :
I become pale and disfigured <note>original: 'ungestalt', referring to the physical wasting away or loss of form caused by dread.</note>
By the length of your years;
I am astonished and shall soon die
Before the multitude of your torments!
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->2.<-

Measure all the drops that are in the sea /
In rivers and in wells;
Count all those that have fallen from above
And those that yet can fall :
Add to them all the flakes
That the snow has ever given;
Yet this number is but a moment <note>original: 'Nu', an archaic term for a 'nunc' or 'moment'—literally the blink of an eye.</note>
Compared to the eternal life of misery.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->3.<-

Count all the leaves with which ever
The forests have delighted us;
And all the grass that late and early
Time has mown down <note>original: 'abgemeyet' (abgemäht), using the common Baroque metaphor of Time or Death as a reaper with a scythe.</note> :

### Fourth Book.

Even count every single speck of dust
That dances in the sunbeams /
You still will not reach the total
Of Eternity.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->4.<-

Imagine a mountain whose peak
Touches the fortress of heaven /
And whose strong roots
Extend as far as the world goes;
Then carry away a single little grain <note>original: 'Gränelein', a diminutive of grain. This metaphor of a bird or person removing one grain of a mountain every thousand years became a famous folk illustration of eternity, later appearing in the Brothers Grimm's fairy tale 'The Shepherd Boy'.</note>
Every thousand years /
Yet the eternal torment remains
As fresh as ever / even when the mountain is gone. <note>original: 'munter', which usually means cheerful or awake, but here signifies that the suffering remains 'vivid' or 'active' without exhaustion.</note>
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->5.<-

Fill the entire firmament <term>Firmament: The sphere of the fixed stars; in Baroque cosmology, the visible canopy of the heavens.</term>
As densely as you can with numbers;
Then let the earth to its very end
Be painted over with digits :
Speak the sum as your mind is able /
Yet you will still not name
The year in which the first day
Of eternity shall break.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->6.<-

Eternity is like a circle <note>original: 'Kreiß'. In early modern German, this term refers to a circle or orb, symbolizing something with no beginning and no end.</note>
That turns within itself;
Like a snake that with diligence
Stands coiled upon itself: <note>This imagery evokes the 'Ouroboros,' an ancient symbol of a snake swallowing its own tail, frequently used in Baroque art to represent the cyclical and infinite nature of time.</note>
It is like a wheel that on and on /
Swings around its axle;
And yet, as long as it lasts,
It brings no call toward the harbor. <note>original: 'Port'. In the 17th century, the 'harbor' was a standard metaphor for the peace of death or the arrival in Heaven after the stormy sea of life. Here, the poet laments that in eternity, one never reaches that final destination.</note>
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->7.<-

It is a fire whose heat
Consumes its very own;
A blaze that through a special art
Feeds upon its own smoke:
It is a throat and a gullet
That constantly swallows itself;
It is an abyss without a bottom <term>Abgrund ohne Grund: Literally a 'groundless ground.' This is a favorite rhetorical device of German mystics and poets to describe the terrifying or divine infinite.</term>
That always moves deeper.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->8.<-

When you think it is now over
After a hundred thousand ages,
Then it only just enters
Its house of mourning for the first time:

# Fourth Book

When it ends, it then begins;
Its beginning is forever;
Its middle it shall never see,
Nor see its end, no, never.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->9.<-

It is a monstrous, glowing fire <note>original: 'ungeheure Glut'. While 'Glut' can mean embers, in the Baroque context of hellfire, it implies a massive, inescapable heat.</note>
That burns past all endurance;
A cutting sword that heart and blood,
That body and soul dissevers:
It is a worm that day and night
Within the conscience gnaweth; <note>This is a biblical allusion to Mark 9:48 ("where their worm dieth not"), representing the internal torment of regret and guilt in the afterlife.</note>
It is a sting that with great force
Pierces the heart and plagues it.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

->10.<-

It is a thunder and a flash
That terrifies, sans comfort;
A ray that with a subtle heat <note>original: 'subtiler Hiz'. In 17th-century natural philosophy, 'subtle' described a substance so fine or refined—like lightning or spirit—that it could penetrate solid objects to destroy them from within.</note>
Doth penetrate and smother:
A storm that all which hope is called
Strikes to the ground in fury;
A tempest that within the spirit
Stirs an eternal woe.
Alas / alas, what is eternity!

# Spiritual Shepherd-Songs

### 11.

It is a horror, a chasm
That appalls the sight;
A deep hole and a dark vault
That cuts off every path:
It is a dungeon <term>Kärker: A dungeon or prison cell, typically underground.</term> that the shine
Of the sun never greets;
A shackle <note>The original "Fässel" likely refers to "Fessel" (shackle/chain), though the spelling suggests a vessel or vat; the context of dragging one's marrow and bone implies an inescapable physical restraint.</note> which marrow and bone
Drags into itself without release.
Alas, alas, what is eternity!

### 12.

It is a bloodthirsty tyrant <term>Wüttrich: A particularly violent or bloodthirsty despot; a common Baroque term for a cruel ruler.</term> and a despot,
An eternal breaker of hearts;
A cruel beast and an angry man,
A strict avenger of sins:
It is a howling and a crying,
An eternal misery of the soul;
An eternal malediction <term>vermaledeyn: From the Latin 'maledicere,' meaning to curse or damn solemnly.</term>,
An eternal condemner!
Alas, alas, what is eternity!

### 13.

Say what you will, eternity
Will never be fully described;
Who knows the height of the cruelty
That it is accustomed to commit:

#### Fourth Book.

No eye has seen its abyss <note>original: "Schlund"; this word can mean an abyss, a whirlpool, or the gaping maw of a monster, often used in this period to describe the entrance to Hell.</note>,
No ear has heard its roaring;
Its torment and its writhing <note>original: "drehn"; literally "turning" or "twisting," referring to the internal churning of agony or the literal twisting of a body in pain.</note>

Angelus Silesius <note>pseudonym of Johann Scheffler</note>. **SACRED SOUL-DELIGHT** / or **SPIRITUAL PASTORAL SONGS** / of the Soul <note>Original: *Psyche*</note> in love with her Jesus. Sung by Johann Angelo Silesio, and adorned with exceptionally beautiful melodies by Mr. Georg Joseph... <note>Original title: *Heilige Seelen-Lust / oder Geistreiche Hirtenlieder / der in ihren Jesu verliebten Psyche*</note> Breslau, Baumann, 1657. $4,000

FIRST EDITION. Four parts in one volume. Engraved frontispiece, title page, 6 leaves, 402 pages; 3 leaves, title page, 123 pages. Featuring music in diamond-shaped notes <note>a style of musical notation common in the Renaissance and Baroque periods</note>, printed typographically. Octavo <note>8vo</note>, contemporary vellum binding. Some foxing <note>age-related spotting on paper</note> and old waterstains, hinges of the binding have cracks. The engraved frontispiece shows the figure of a woman with a lute (representing the soul) in a landscape, with light descending upon her from heaven.

Angelus Silesius (1624-1677) is one of the most remarkable characters in the literature of the 17th century. Originally he belonged to the Protestant mystic circles centered around Abraham von Franckenberg and Daniel von Czepko. In 1653 he converted to Roman Catholicism. He became a fighter for the Counter-Reformation, first as a layman and a member of the Rosicrucian Brotherhood; in 1661 he became a priest. **SACRED SOUL-DELIGHT** <note>Original: *Heilige Seelenlust*</note>, the first of his two principal works, has as its subject the love of the "Bride-Soul" for Christ. Most of the songs were incorporated by both Protestants and Catholics into their songbooks. The composer of the melodies, Georg Joseph, a musician in the service of the prince-bishop of Breslau, worked closely together with the poet.
